title: Molecular fence Cu-based catalyst for CO_2 hydrogenation to CO with high activity and durability

paper_content.abstract:
The conversion of CO into high-value syngas (CO and H ) using Cu-based catalysts has garnered
2 2
considerable interest. However, these catalysts deactivate rapidly due to Ostwald-ripening and thermal
aggregation. Herein, we propose to encapsulate Cu-cluster into mMOR zeolite for engineering a
separation-site catalyst Cu@mMOR. In the reverse water-gas shift reaction (RWGS), mMOR zeolite of
Cu@mMOR directly captures and then activates CO , and simultaneously serves as a molecular fence to
2
prevent CO contact with Cu-clusters surrounding with small pore of mMOR (< 3.0 Å) channels. These
2
encapsulated Cu-clusters in mMOR possess considerable Cu vacancies, which significantly facilitate H
2
heterolytic dissociation, transferring H* species towNards activated CO
2
on mMOR and converting them
into CO. This separation-site strategy efficientl y increases catalytic activation while intelligently altering
2
the CO reaction pathway, preventing Cu from thermal agglomeration and Oswald ripening in the catalyst.
2
Consequently, Cu@mMOR attainTs a space-time yield of CO as high as 3290 mmol g -1 h-1, with catalytic
cat
stability extending up to 7A88 hours.
paper_content.introduction:
The ongoing and excessive emissions of CO have led to global climate change, which is currently
2
receiving considerable attention. The conversion of CO into high-value chemicals is essential for
2
mitigating the greenhouse effect and maintaining a sustainable environment and energy supply1. Among
these, syngas (CO and H mixture) is reported to be an essential chemical used in the large-scale
2
production of alcohols, esters, and liquid fuels2. Recently, the insufficient provision stemming from
reliance solely on fossil resources has spurred growing interest in catalytic CO hydrogenation-a
2
promising strategy for converting greenhouse gases into valuable syngas3. Despite its apparent appeal,
this approach presents formidable obstacles.

The reverse water-gas shift reaction (RWG S) is a desirable and promising CCU technology that
catalytically converts CO into syngas under a H environment. Operating the RWGS at atmospheric
2 C 2
pressure and temperatures abovTe 500 °C enables direct conversion of CO into syngas with the ideal
2
H /CO ratio for Fischer-TAropsch synthesis, requiring only moderate energy input and avoiding extra
2
downstream separation4. For this reaction, Cu-based catalysts are promising non-noble metal candidates
for RWGS because of their high hydrogenation activity and high CO selectivity5. In general, high
temperature during the RWGS reaction usually tends to lead to the sintering of Cu, which can result in
catalyst deactivation via the aggregation of Cu NPs. Encapsulating the active metal inside thermally robust
zeolites is an effective way to curb high-temperature aggregation. For instance, Xiao et al. embedded Pt
NPs within Beta zeolite via a seed-mediated growth route, constructing a rigid “protective shell” around
the Pt that markedly suppressed thermal migration and aggregation6. Likewise, Liu et al. confined sub-
nanometer Pt clusters in the straight channels of MEL zeolite, firmly anchoring the naked Pt species and
achieving excellent stability in methyl-cyclohexane dehydrogenation7. These reports confirm that zeolite-
confinement can efficiently mitigate thermally induced particle aggregation. However, high-temperature
sintering can also proceed via an Ostwald-ripening path, where volatile metal species migrate from
interior pores to the outer surface and aggregate. For example, Julian et al. reported that confined Mo
zeolite still diffuses outward during high-temperature methane dehydrogenation, causing agglomeration
and coking8. Analogous to the above catalysts, Cu species are susceptible to forming volatile Cu-carbonyl
complexes under CO-rich conditions, leading to significant catalyst deactivation9. Therefore, the
simultaneous inhibition of Ostwald-ripening alongside the migration and aggregation of Cu species in the
RWGS reaction remains a crucial challenge for acNhieving high-performance catalysts that exhibit both
efficient activation and enduring stability.

Herein, we proposed to construct Cu@mMOR (copper-encapsulated modified mordenite zeolite) that
encapsulate Cu clusters within TmMOR (modified mordenite zeolite) crystals to realize catalytic site
separation for CO and H A activation in RWGS reaction. For our designed catalyst, mMOR was triggered
2 2
to crystallize around Cu clusters and encapsulate Cu species insides via its Na+-induced crystallized small
pore channels (< 3.0 Å) linking with Cu-O bonds. CO was efficiently captured and activated on outside
2
mMOR, which served as the molecular fence to isolated CO from Cu clusters depended on its small
2
channels. On the other hand, H was dissociated into H* on internal Cu clusters and spillover toward
2
activated CO via Cu-O interface of Cu@mMOR, and finally produced CO with high selectivity. The
2
catalytic site separation strategy significantly enhanced catalytic activation for both CO and H , and
2 2
rationally changed the CO reaction pathway, thereby effectively preventing Cu Oswald ripening and
2
thermal aggregation in catalysts. Therefore, a space-time yield of 3290 mmol g -1 h-1 was attained in
cat
Cu@mMOR at high-temperature conditions (600 °C), showcasing the long-term stability of catalyst
performance over a duration of 788 hours (49.1% CO -conversion-rate and 99.6% CO-selectivity).
2

Design idea and synthesis strategy for Cu@mMOR
Fig. 1 showed our design idea and the corresponding synthesis strategy for mMOR-confined Cu catalyst
(denoted as Cu@mMOR) having separated catalytic sites for H and CO . Firstly, SiO nanospheres were
2 2 2
used to encapsulate Cu-based precursor via a reversed-phase micro-emulsion method (seen Fig. 1a-b).
Next, Cu-based precursor were calcined and reduced into Cu particles surrounding with SiO (named
2
Cu@SiO ,Fig. 1c). In this process, Na+ was used as a directing agent to induce the growth of small Si-O
2
cages (< 3.0 Å) in mMOR to isolate CO from Cu species. Next, the whole part of SiO of Cu@SiO was
2 2 2
gradually converted into mMOR zeolite under the iNnduction of N-methyl-pyrrolidine and followed by the
second calcination and H reduction (seen Fig. 1d-f and Supplementary Fig. 1). Finally, a portion of Na+
2
was selectively retained while the remainder was converted to NH + via low-concentration NH Cl
4 4
exchange, followed by calcinatioTn to ultimately form H⁺, resulting in the formation of Cu@mMOR.

Morphology of different Cu-based catalysts
It is evident from Fig. 2a-b that Cu@mMOR contained numerous Cu black dots (1.5 ± 0.3 nm) that were
homogenously dispersed throughout the nanosheets. These amorphous Cu nanodots were encapsulated in
mMOR, which was identified by the lattice fringes of (110) plane10 (Fig. 2c). According to the elemental
energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)-mapping images depicted in Fig. 2d, the Cu element was
homogeneously distributed throughout the mMOR zeolite. However, the particle size of Cu in spherical
Cu@SiO (~20 nm, Fig. 2e) was about ~2.1 nm (Fig. 2f), which was obviously larger than that in
2
Cu@mMOR. It can be inferred that Cu was further reduced into smaller clusters in a confined space
during the crystal transformation from SiO to mMOR. In contrast, Cu-impregnated mMOR (denoted as
2
Cu/mMOR) contained nano-sized particles of approximately 4.4 nm on its outer surface of mMOR (Fig.
2g), and these nanoparticles displayed distinct lattice patterns corresponding to the metallic Cu (111)
crystal plane11 (Fig. 2h). It can be seen that the copper acetylacetonate impregnation method proved
challenging for incorporating Cu nanoparticles into mMOR crystals and effectively controlling their
particle size within mMOR.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyses (Supplementary Fig. 2 and
Supplementary Table 1) revealed that Cu/mMOR and Cu@mMOR had high crystallinity of MOR type
zeolite, whereas Cu@SiO showed a diffuse X-ray peak of amorphous silica phase. This indicated that
2
the amorphous silica nanosphere was completely transformed into a highly crystalline MOR zeolite
structure in Cu@mMOR12. In addition, non e of the three catalysts (Cu@SiO , Cu/mMOR, and
2
Cu@mMOR) showed clear diffraction peaks of Cu crystals. However, the Cu element detected in XRF
(Supplementary Table 1) had aT very similar percentage composition in the range of 2.6-4.1 wt.%,
suggesting that Cu speciAes were highly dispersed in these catalysts. Additionally, the XPS survey
(Supplementary Fig. 3) showed the slight presence of Na element in Cu@mMOR but not in Cu/mMOR,
implying that the former remains some Na+ sites. Moreover, the Cu 2p XPS patterns of Cu@mMOR and
Cu@SiO exhibited much lower peak area than that of impregnated Cu/mMOR (Supplementary Fig. 4),
2
suggesting the extensive encapsulation of Cu nanoparticles rather than their exposure on the MOR
external surface13. Next, the pore texture (Supplementary Fig. 5 and Supplementary Table 2) of
Cu@mMOR showed a slight reduction in N adsorption uptake (427.1 m2 g-1) of type I isotherm compared
2
to that of pure mMOR (530.1 m2 g-1). This meant that most of the micropore structure of mMOR
maintained upon encapsulating Cu nanoparticles in mMOR. In contrast, Cu/mMOR exhibited a lower
surface area of 310.7 m2 g-1, indicating a partial loss of the mMOR porous structure due to the obstruction
caused by the impregnated Cu nanoparticles14. As anticipated, Cu@SiO had minimal porous structures
2
attributed to the low porosity of SiO . The textural structure analysis inferred that Cu@mMOR maintained
2
the mMOR porous property after encapsulating Cu species with homogeneous distribution, which would
favor the adsorption and transport of reactants and active species during the reaction. Further, positron
annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS) was conducted to determine the pore size distribution of the
ultra-microporous region in MOR, mMOR, and their Cu-based catalysts15. The deconvoluted PALS
spectra display four distinct peaks corresponding to different positron annihilation lifetimes (τ -τ ;
1 4
Supplementary Fig. 6a). An increase in τ value indNicates larger pore sizes within the MOR framework.
Here, τ denotes the bulk lifetime, which is attrib uted to direct annihilation within the non-porous regions16.

The remaining lifetimes τ -τ correspond to positron annihilation within the 5-membered, 8-membered,

and 12-membered ring channels Tof MOR, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 6b-c). In comparison to the

Å)19. Conceptually, this double-ring encapsulation architecture could act as a "molecular fence" for

Structural characterization of different Cu-based catalysts
To better understand the local structure of Cu species in different micro-environments, X-ray absorption
spectroscopy (XAS) was performed in order to evaluate the Cu chemical state and coordination status in
various catalysts. The edge energy of the two catalysts (Cu@mMOR and Cu/mMOR) at the Cu K-edge
(Fig. 3a) was positioned between the Cu foil and CuN2 O standards, with no pre-edge band of Cu2+ detected
in the rising edge. This implied that Cu species were in the form of Cu0 and Cu+ rather than Cu2+ in the
two catalysts20. Compared to Cu/mMOR, Cu@mMOR exhibited a much higher Cu adsorption edge
energy, attributing to a higher proTportion of Cu+ species in Cu@mMOR21. To quantify the Cu+ species in
the catalyst, a mathematicAal relationship between the absorption edge energy position and the valence
state was established by fitting data from the corresponding standards22, 23. As shown in Supplementary
Fig. 8, the Cu+ content in Cu@mMOR was calculated to be ⁓38.1 at.%. In contrast, the Cu+ proportions
in Cu/mMOR and Cu@SiO were determined to be only 9.0 and 6.9 at.%, respectively. The significantly
2
higher Cu+ content in Cu@mMOR is indicative of enhanced interfacial charge transfer from Cu0 to
mMOR, a process facilitated by the abundant interfaces inherent to the encapsulation structure.

The local coordination environment of Cu species in various catalysts was identified by fitting the
Fourier transform extended X-ray absorption fine structure (FT-EXAFS) of the various catalysts, as
illustrated in Fig. 3b. As shown, Cu@mMOR exhibited a notable Cu-O peak at 1.46 Å, as well as minor
Cu-O-Cu and Cu-Cu peaks at 2.57 and 2.08 Å, respectively, indicating that most of its Cu species were
coordinated with O within Cu@mMOR24. Furthermore, the wavelet transform (WT) plot of Cu@mMOR
in Fig. 3c-1 showed an obvious Cu-O bond (k = 3.2-5.6 Å-1, R = 1.8-1.9 Å) and a weak Cu-Cu bond (k =
6.2-7.4 Å-1, R = 2.1-2.7 Å) when compared to Cu O (Fig. 3c-2) and Cu foil (Fig. 3c-3) counterparts25,
2
corroborating the results from the FT-EXAFS spectra. The shell fitting analysis presented in
Supplementary Table 3 depicts that most of the copper in Cu@mMOR coordinated with oxygen (O) and
formed Cu-O clusters, with only a small amount of Cu-Cu bonding remaining26. The XANES, FT-EXAFS,
and WT plot results proved that Cu-O clusters dominated the main position in the Cu@mMOR, with a
small portion of metallic Cu clusters in mMOR. Differently, Cu/mMOR and Cu@SiO
2
(Supplementary
Fig. 9) displayed significant similarities to Cu- foil in their EXAFS and WT plot features, reflecting the
predominant presence of metallic Cu0 with larger nanoparticle sizes in Cu/mMOR and Cu@SiO .
2
From the above results, the schematic rTepresentation of Cu@mMOR formation is illustrated in Fig. 3d. Initially,
the SiO in Cu@SiO begAan to crystallize into mMOR. Then, Cu grains confined in mMOR underwent
2 2
mMOR compression and tore into smaller Cu nanoclusters. During this process, confined space
continuously generated strong interactions between Cu and silanol, resulting in enrichment of the Cu-O
coordination within mMOR. Thus, Cu@mMOR contained abundant Cu-O clusters with atomic
distribution in the mMOR crystal. Conversely, this character was not observed for Cu/mMOR due to the
lack of the in situ mMOR crystallization process.

Moreover, the types and contents of defects in Cu clusters within Cu@mMOR were investigated via
UV-Raman spectroscopy, with the results shown in Fig. 3e. As seen, the confined Cu@mMOR exhibited
a sharp peak at 221 cm-1 and a broad peak around 400-463 cm-1, corresponding to the defective Cu-O of
Cu vacancies (the missing Cu atom in Cu-O-Cu motifs) and Si-O of MOR framework, respectively27, 28.
In comparison, Cu/mMOR displayed a negligible peak of defective Cu-O around Cu vacancies at 218 cm-
1 and a minor peak of Si-O of MOR at 397 cm-1. The intensities of these peaks indicated that Cu@mMOR
had a much higher concentration of Cu vacancies than Cu/mMOR, which was attributed to the Cu-O
defective coordination during the crystallization of mMOR from SiO . Additionally, Raman spectra
2
(Supplementary Fig. 10) were also measured for Cu@mMOR and Cu@SiO . As observed, the defective
2
Cu-O around Cu vacancies had a significantly higher peak intensity with a blue shift from 215 to 221 cm-
1 in Cu@mMOR compared to Cu@SiO . This once again demonstrated that the lattice compression of
2
crystal transformation induced the contraction of CNu-O bonds in Cu clusters, resulting in the generation
of additional Cu vacancies29.

It has been reported that Cu vacancies can significantly influence the redox properties of catalysts30, 31.
Furthermore, H temperature-pTrogrammed reduction-mass spectrometry (H -TPR-MS) analyses of
2 2
various catalysts were caArried out to investigate the redox properties of Cu. Initially, all catalysts
underwent complete oxidation to CuO prior to measurement. Fig. 3f showed the TPR-MS profiles of
Cu@mMOR and Cu/mMOR. As shown, hydrogen reduction profile of Cu@mMOR exhibited a single
hydrogen reduction peak at 262°C, whereas the corresponding peak for Cu/mMOR appeared at a higher
temperature (ca. 300°C). This significant shift to a lower temperature suggested that the copper species in
Cu@mMOR possessed smaller sizes and higher reducibility32. To quantitatively assess the hydrogen
spillover effect, the hydrogen spillover capacity was determined by calculating the additional H
2
consumption beyond that used for water formation. The results showed that each Cu atom in Cu@mMOR
consumed an extra 0.45 H atoms, while the Cu/mMOR exhibited almost no additional H consumption
2
(0.01 H/Cu). These results suggest that a significant hydrogen spillover phenomenon occurred in
Cu@mMOR, thereby demonstrating that the synergy between its confined microenvironment and copper
vacancies effectively promotes H activation and spillover.
2

Importantly, the electron transfer induced by metal vacancies can alter the surface acidic properties of
support33. In order to better understand this effect, NH -TPD (Supplementary Fig. 12) was performed to
3
explore the acidic concentration and acidity of mMOR in various catalysts. As displayed, pristine mMOR

250 ºC) acids34. Compared to pristine mMOR, Cu@mMOR showed a notable reduction in total acid
content to 197 μmol g-1, with the retained portNion almost composed of strong acids. Conversely,
Cu/mMOR exhibited a slight reduction in all a cids, yielding a total value of 398 μmol g-1. Furthermore,

of catalysts, as shown in SupplemTentary Fig. 13. Compared to Cu/mMOR, Cu@mMOR demonstrated a

3
(Supplementary Fig. 12). As calculated, its strong BAS ratio in total BAS was up to 81.7%, far higher

Meanwhile, this charge transfer could further enable Cu@mMOR to retain more Na+ sites (mentioned in
Supplementary Fig. 3), which are stabilized by stronger electrostatic interactions towards O of
Cu@mMOR37.

To further understand the structural evolution of Cu species during the long-term reaction process, the
structure and morphology of fresh catalysts and spent catalysts after 120 h reaction were determined by
using XRD and TEM, as shown in Fig. 4f-h. Spent Cu/mMOR displayed obvious diffraction peaks at 43°
and 51° assigned to metallic Cu bulks53, which did not appear in the fresh samples. This suggested that
the local aggregation of Cu increased with reaction time. On the other hand, no distinct Cu diffraction
peaks were found in spent Cu@mMOR, implying a high dispersion of Cu species within mMOR.
Additionally, TEM images revealed that Cu species in fresh and spent Cu@mMOR had nearly the same
particle size of approximately 2 nm. In the case of Cu/mMOR, the Cu nanoparticles increased in size from
an initial range of 3-6 nm in the fresh sample to a range of 15-33 nm in the spent sample. Taking account
of these above characterizations, the sintering of Cu species was the main cause of the Cu/mMOR
deactivation.

Cu@SiO was prepared by a modified reported method from the literature91. Briefly, 3.37 g of Brij-58
2

demulsify the microemulsion. The mixture was centrifuged to obtaiSn the precipitate (8000 rpm, with a
relative centrifugal force of 5800 g), which was dried in a vacuum oven at 70 °C for 12 hours. The dried
powder was then calcined at 500 °C in an air stream to remRove organic species. During calcination, the
temperature was increased slowly at a rate of 1 °C per minute to avoid the formation of quartz phases and
to prevent the rapid diffusion of decomposition gases, which could create excessive meso-porosity.
Eventually, the product Cu@SiO was reduced at 773 K for 3 hours under a 30 mL/min flow of 5% H in
2 E 2
N .

(1.28 g), aqueous sodium hydroxide (8.6 g, 30 wt.%), and deionized water (66.37 g) in a homogenizer at

Cu@SiO .

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In the present study, the authors designed a strategy of catalytic function separation to achieve highly efficient and durable CO2 hydrogenation to CO over Cu-based catalysts. Specifically, Cu nanoparticles were confined within the micropores of MOR zeolite, making these Cu sites only accessible to H2 dissociation but not to CO2 hydrogenation. Na+ cations residing in the channel of MOR were supposed by the authors as active sites to catalyze CO2 hydrogenation with H* species transferred from the separated Cu nanoparticles via hydrogen spillover. Although the proposed strategy is attractive and a seemingly excellent performance has been obtained for CO2 hydrogenation on the designed Cu@mMOR catalyst, I am concerned that some of the conclusions lack compelling evidence, particularly regarding the role of Na⁺ ions as efficient active sites for CO₂ hydrogenation. I am afraid I cannot recommend the publication of this manuscript in Nature Communications at least with the current content. My main concerns are addressed as follows.
1. The authors claimed that Cu nanoparticles confined within the micropores of MOR zeolite were not accessible to CO2 and CO molecules. This conclusion was reached mainly based on the weak H2-TPR signals for the N2O-treated Cu@mMOR sample (Fig. 5a). However, it is well known the N2O treatment at mild temperatures can only oxidize metallic Cu to Cu+, and Figure 3 shows that the Cu+ species had already prevailed in the Cu@mMOR sample before the N2O treatment, indicating the Cu species was not able to be further oxidized in the N2O treatment. Therefore, the weak signals observed in the H2-TPR experiment are unsurprising, and this evidence is invalid to prove the inaccessibility of CO2 to the Cu surface.
2. Related to the above issue, it is indeed surprising to see that Cu species in the Cu@mMOR sample cannot be reduced fully to the metallic state even the temperature in the H2-TPR process increased to 873 K (Figure 3f). Could the authors provide an explanation on this phenomenon? It is also suggested to quantify the H2 consumption per Cu atom in the H2-TPR shown in Figure 3f.
3. It is noticeable that the authors removed most of Na+ cations in the synthesized Cu@mMOR catalyst via ion exchange with NH4Cl, while they claimed that the residual Na+ cations served as the active sites for catalyzing CO2 hydrogenation. I am afraid the authors need to examine whether the residual Na+ cations are exchangeable with NH4+ and whether the amount of the Na+ cations can correlate with the hydrogenation rate of CO2.
4. What is the rate-determining step in CO2 hydrogenation over the Cu@mMOR catalyst? The authors did not make an unambiguous assessment. In general, the dissociation of H2 is a fast step on Cu, and the cleavage of C-O bond in CO2 is crucial. The authors showed the possible occurrence of CO2 hydrogenation on the Na+ sites via DFT calculations, while they did not demonstrate the hydrogenation can occur faster on the Na+ sites than on the Cu surface, which would be the basis for the excellent catalytic performance of Cu@mMOR. Moreover, if the Na+ cations are the key active sites for CO2 hydrogenation, how will the authors explain the better catalytic activity of Cu@SiO2 compared with that of Cu/MOR?
5. The authors stated that CO2 hydrogenation on the Na+ cations preferred the formate pathway (via the HCOO* intermediate) over the carboxyl pathway (via the COOH* intermediate). The DFT evidence provided by the authors is not convincible. They only showed that the formation of HCOO* from CO2 possesses a lower activation barrier than that for the formation of COOH*, while they did not examine the activation barriers for their decompositions into CO* and OH*. It seems that the decomposition of HCOO* is much more difficult because it requires the cleavages of the C-H and C-O bonds at the same time.
6. What is the nature of H* species transferred from the Cu sites to the Na+ sites via the hydrogen spillover, a radical or a proton? Generally, the diffusion of protons in the zeolite is much easier, but CO2 hydrogenation cannot be completed only with protons.
7. Regarding the catalytic performance, the durability test for Cu@mMOR was conducted under a condition close to reaction equilibrium (Figure 4d). In such a case, the amount of catalyst is overqualified, making it unsuitable to assess the true catalyst stability. Similarly, the strong dependence of CO2 hydrogenation rate on the space velocity (Figure 4c) indicates the rate measurement was not within the reaction-controlled regime.
8. The authors are recommended to provide clear definitions for mMOR and Cu vacancy before using or discussing these concepts in the manuscript.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This paper deals with the selective hydrogenation of CO2 to CO over copper clusters encapsulated in mMOR zeolite (denoted as Cu@mMOR) at 600 °C. The catalysts achieved performances markedly superior to that of recently reported in the literature, with a space-time yield of CO as high as 3290 mmol gcat-1 h-1, a CO selectivity of up to 99.6% and a catalytic stability extending up to 788 hours. To comprehend how the catalyst works the authors compared its properties with those of mMOR impregnated (Cu/mMOR) or SiO2 encapsulated (Cu@SiO2) copper nanoparticles respectively. The bulk and surface properties of the catalysts were analyzed by several techniques (X-ray absorption spectroscopy, Fourier transform extended X-ray absorption fine structure, X-ray Absorption Near Edge Structure, UV-Raman spectroscopy, H2-TPR, H2-TPD, NH3-TPD, CO2-TPD, H/D exchange. The hydrogenation of CO2 was conducted in a flow-bed reactor. The reaction paths were investigated by DRIFTS-tests and simulated by ab initio calculations.
Cu@mMOR was prepared from Cu@SiO2 precursor obtained by reversed-phase micro-emulsion method. Na+ ions induced the formation of small cages (  3 nm) in the zeolite structure and also ensured a better separation of metal and oxide phases. Copper species were in the form of Cu0 and Cu+ rather than Cu2+ with a higher proportion of Cu+ species in Cu@mMOR. Most of the copper in Cu@mMOR coordinated with oxygen and formed Cu-O clusters, with only a small amount of Cu-Cu bonding remaining. The interactions of copper with the O atoms of mMOR were the strongest and gave rise to a better dispersion of copper sites and their isolation from mMOR sites. In contrast, the presence of metallic Cu0 with larger nanoparticle sizes was predominant in Cu/mMOR and Cu@SiO2. Cu@mMOR had a much higher concentration of Cu vacancies than Cu/mMOR. Moreover, additional Cu vacancies were generated by the contraction of Cu-O bonds in Cu clusters induced by the lattice compression. Brönsted acidity of mMOR notably diminished in Cu@MOR as compared to Cu/mMOR, however with the retained portion almost composed of strong acids. Cu@mMOR exhibited great amounts of hydrogen spillover incorporated and strong interactions between CO2 and Na+.
Based on the above information (characterization and testings) the reaction pathway for Cu@mMOR was deduced as follows: CO2 was first captured on the Na+ sites of mMOR, then reduced by spillover H* to HCOO*, and finally formed CO and H2O.
Comments:
This is an excellent paper describing an original method of selective hydrogenation of CO2 to CO, a hot topic in both academic and applied research. The catalyst prepared exhibited higher performances than that recently reported in the literature The conclusions on the structural properties of the catalysts are supported by the use of a wide range of appropriate physical and physicochemical tools of fresh and spent catalysts. The results may be reproduced. It fulfills the standards required in heterogeneous catalysis. However, it presents some weaknesses.
First, the content of the manuscript is an illustration of the hydrogen spillover effect in the case of hydrogenation reactions over zeolite encapsulated metal catalysts. Also the work of authors dealing with this topic should be cited (e. g. Choi et al., Nat. Commun. 2014; ChemCatChem. 2015).
Second, the role of Na+ ions and the triggering of the reaction are unclear.
Indeed, according to the authors, these ions would form an additional sublayer strenghening the separation between copper and the support shell, preventing any contact between the former and CO2 (Figure 1d). However, a strong interaction was evidenced between the sodium ions and CO2. This is a contradiction, unless some sodium ions exist at the zeolite surface. In such a case, CO2, as a Lewis acid, would be adsorbed on surface O atoms or OH hydroxyls of the zeolite, forming (hydrogeno)carbonate species. In the presence of surface Na+ ions it would interact with surface ONa species forming carbonate entities. Such entities were not evidenced by the authors.
This point should be clarified.
A reasonable pathway would be the direct reaction of CO2 with H spiltover species forming the formate species evidenced by the authors. In this way it is worth noting the recent claim (Bettahar, Catal. Rev., 2022; Catalysts, 2024) that the structure of hydrogen spillover in the case of non-reducible oxide supports consists in surface Hδ-/OHδ+ (0<δ<1) pairs resulting from the adsorption of the H spiltover species on conjugated Mm+ Op- (p=1 or 2) pairs. The conjugated pairs pre-exist in basic (e.g. MgO) or amphoteric (e.g. alumina) oxide supports. For hydroxylated/acidic supports (silica, alumina, zeolites) they are formed by a dehydroxylation process during the catalyst reduction. The reaction between the hydridic fragment of Hδ-/OHδ+ pairs and CO2 would produce formate species which are further decomposed to CO and H2O by the protonic fragment:
+CO2
Mm+Op- + 2 Hspilt <=> M(m- δ)+Hδ- O(p- δ)-Hδ+ => M(m- δ)+HCOO δ- O(p- δ)Hδ+ =>=> Mm+Op- + CO+H2O
Finally the above considerations pose the question of the effect of the degree of protonation of the zeolite on the Cu@mMOR catalyst performances? Would this degree beneficial or detrimental to the catalyst activity? The answer to this question may help the comprehending of the structural and chemical role of the Na+ ions.
In conclusion, the submitted article is of high experimental and theoretical level. As a whole, the interpretations of the results are very good, except that related to the role of the additional layer of Na+ ions. References should be completed. Therefore it may be published in Nature Communications with a revision tacking into account the above remarks.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Authors report a highly active and selective Cu catalysts for high-T RWGS. It is an interesting case study to push toward the equilibrium limit. The characterizations and DFT studies help to gain understanding of active sites and mechanism.
However, the significance of current study is not clear.
1. Synthesis of particles in a confined spaces has been reported previously to limit aggregation under reaction. These studies need to be cited and discussed to highlight the significant contribution from current study as compared to the previous.
2. RWGS on Cu or Cu-based catalysts has been extensively studied. Under CO2 and H2, Cu alone is known to produce CO as the major product. Although the high selectivity is reported here, the reaction temperature is very high compared to the typical. It is not surprising that increased temperature promote CO2 conversion and decomposition of methanol to CO, thus increasing CO selectivity. What is the benefit of this high-T RWGS inconsideration of energy cost?
3. Apparent activation energies reported for three systems are all below 1 eV. It is not straightforward that such low barrier requires high temperatures (> 450C) to overcome.
4. Surface of MOR was simulated. Why? How representative to the cage structure of MOR?
5. It was reported that formate is very stable on Cu. The barrier for formate decomposition to CO needs to be calculated. In addition, the barriers for competitive hydrogenations to *HCOOH and *H2COO should also be compared to ensure the claimed pathway. Without that, the current conclusion is not convincing.
6. There is no structure in Supplementary Fig. 20-21.

Author reply: Thank the reviewer for the thoughtful comment. We agree with your speculation regarding the N O-H -TPR experiment. However, in this work, our Cu@mMOR catalyst is proved to contain a considerable amount of Cu0, which was not clearly confirmed in our original manuscript. This ambiguity likely led the reviewer to misinterpret the weak H -TPR signals as insufficient evidence for the interaction between CO and Cu nanoparticles.
Therefore, in the revised manuscript, (1) we have clearly identified the proportions of Cu0 and Cu+ in each catalyst based on the white-line peak intensities (newly added Supplementary Fig. 6). (2) To further demonstrate the “molecular fence” effect of Cu@mMOR, we have added Si solid-state NMR (newly added Supplementary Fig. 14) characterization for Cu@mMOR to prove the isolation of CO from Cu nanoparticles. (3) We supplied content in CO -DRIFTS spectra in Fig. 5b via CO reaction with Cu nanoparticles.
The revised sections and supplying contents (Three Parts) were highlighted in the revised manuscript and shown as following:
Part I:
Added part of the 1st derivative patterns of white-line (Supplementary Fig. 6), revised manuscript, page 9: “Furthermore, the Cu+ proportion of various catalysts was linearly correlated with the white-line peak location of standard samplesR1. Author reply: The residual presence of Na ions is an intentional design in our preparation process to enhance the adsorption and activation of CO by the molecular sieve. In response to your inquiry, our reply is as follows:
We adopted a “low-concentration and multi-step” exchange to precisely adjust the Na content in mMOR to prevent all Na ions from being exchanged out. Eventually, the dried sample was followed by air calcination and H reduction at 500 °C to obtain Cu@mMOR.”
Secondly, to answer “whether the amount of the Na+ cations can correlate with the hydrogenation rate of CO ”, we precisely modulated the Na+ content in Cu@mMOR through ion exchange. Author reply: We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion.
(1) The response to the question of “What is the rate-determining step in CO hydrogenation over the Cu@mMOR catalyst?”:
We apologize for not having clearly identified the corresponding rate-determining step in the original manuscript, which led to reviewer confusion. First, we reconstructed a model that more closely represents our catalyst structure. Next, based on the in situ DRIFTS experimental observations, we recalculated the DFT of reaction pathway (see added Fig. 5g). We then correlated these new results with the original KIE data (Supplementary Fig. 38). From this combined analysis, we conclude that the migration of an “H+/H- pair” from the Cu clusters to mMOR is the rate-determining step. The relevant details (KIE and reaction energy barrier) have been added in two paragraphs in the Mechanism section of revised manuscript (Two Parts), as follows:
Part I:
Added and revised manuscript, pages 20: “As shown, the KIE value (r /r ) of Cu@mMOR increased progressively from 1.03 at 300 °C to 1.43 at 600 °C, revealing a pronounced temperature-dependent discrepancy. The significantly elevated KIE value of 1.43 (substantially greater than unity) strongly suggests that H* spillover served as the rate-determining step (RDS) in this reactionR6. This mechanistic distinction set it apart from the RWGS reaction observed in other catalytic systemsR7.”
Part II:

(2) The response to the question of “The authors showed the possible occurrence of CO hydrogenation on the Na+ sites via DFT calculations, while they did not demonstrate the hydrogenation can occur faster on the Na+ sites than on the Cu surface, which would be the basis for the excellent catalytic performance of Cu@mMOR.”:
Our Cu@mMOR catalyst has been confirmed to possess spatially separated CO - and H -activation sites, as demonstrated by N O-H -TPR and CO -DRIFTS analyses (Fig. 5a and Fig. 5b). In this manuscript, metallic Cu clusters dissociate H to generate H⁺/H⁻ species that spill over, whereas the Na⁺ sites within the mordenite framework adsorb CO and drive the subsequent hydrogenation step. These two functions were isolated by the mMOR zeolite channels. Therefore, when the two catalytic sites do not undergo hydrogenation simultaneously, their reaction rates cannot be compared.
(3) The response to the question of “if the Na+ cations are the key active sites for CO hydrogenation, how will the authors explain the better catalytic activity of Cu@SiO compared with that of Cu/MOR?”:
In our system, factors other than Na can also influence the hydrogenation rate. For the Na-free catalysts of Cu@SiO and Cu/mMOR, they serve as references lacking mMOR and lacking encapsulated structure, respectively. Thus, they do not possess the significance for making direct comparisons. The superior CO hydrogenation performance exhibited by Cu@SiO may originate from its smaller catalyst particles, higher Cu content, and the more Cu-O interaction at the interface, etc.
5. The authors stated that CO hydrogenation on the Na+ cations preferred the formate pathway (via the HCOO* intermediate) over the carboxyl pathway (via the COOH* intermediate). The DFT evidence provided by the authors is not convincible. They only showed that the formation of HCOO* from CO possesses a lower activation barrier than that for the formation of COOH*, while they did not examine the activation barriers for their decompositions into CO* and OH*. It seems that the decomposition of HCOO* is much more difficult because it requires the cleavages of the C-H and C-O bonds at the same time.
Author reply: We thank the reviewer for pointing out the shortcomings in our theoretical calculations.
In response to the “while they did not examine the activation barriers for their decompositions into CO* and OH*.”, we have added the barriers for direct dissociation of HCOO* and COOH* (Fig. 5g), which required high barriers of 1.72 eV and 2.07 eV, respectively. Furthermore, we added the barriers for protonation of HCOO* and dehydration of HCOOH to CO, which possessed lower barriers than the direct dissociation of HCOO*.
To answer “It seems that the decomposition of HCOO* is much more difficult because it requires the cleavages of the C-H and C-O bonds at the same time.”: COOH+ must acquire two electrons from H- during its conversion to CO, making long-range electron transfer energetically unfavorable. In contrast, the decomposition of HCOOH required no additional electron transfer and could form a stable OC-H O transition state via the intramolecular hydrogen transferR8 (Supplementary Movie 8). As a result, the barrier of HCOOH dissociation was lower than that for COOH+.
Accordingly, we have revised the DFT section in the manuscript and highlighted, as follow:
Revised manuscript, pages 21-22: “Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed to investigate the CO hydrogenation mechanism over the Cu@mMOR at the atomic level. As shown in Fig. 5g, H heterolytically dissociated on the Cu cluster, generating active H+ and H- that migrate to the Si-ONa-Al site. Meanwhile, CO was chemisorbed to carbonate at the same site. In this chemisorption configuration, CO * (carbonate species) could be hydrogenated to COOH+ via the carboxyl pathway or to HCOO- via the formate pathway. A comparison of energy barriers exhibited that forming COOH needed 0.98 eV, whereas producing HCOO- required only 0.64 eV. Due to the lower barrier, CO * preferred to follow formate pathway, which was consistent with the DRIFTS observation that detected only the formate intermediate (Fig. 5e). Next, HCOO- faced a competition between direct dissociation and protonation. DFT calculations showed that the barrier of protonation was only 0.43 eV, far below the 1.72 eV needed for direct dissociation. This implied that HCOO- would rapidly protonate to yield HCOOH in Cu@mMOR.”

Author reply: We thank the reviewer for the very valuable question. Meanwhile, we have refined the model and made corresponding revisions to the descriptions regarding the TDOS and Cu-PDOS. Based on these added experiments, we infer that the nature of hydrogen spillover in Cu@mMOR is the migration of H+ and electrons within the mMOR framework and their recombination into H+/H- at Si-ONa-Al sites. Subsequently, H- attacks CO to trigger the RWGS reaction. Accordingly, we have revised the mechanism section in the manuscript and highlighted, as follow:

Author reply: We thank the reviewer for the important comment.
1. During the experimental design phase, we extensively referenced evaluation conditions from high-performance RWGS systems (see comparative analysis in Table S4). To ensure meaningful benchmarking, our reaction conditions were deliberately aligned with mainstream methodologies in the fieldR19-R28.
2. Durability testing under equilibrium conditions is not intrinsically correlated with catalyst overloadingR29. In the kinetically controlled regime, an increase in space velocity reduces the contact time between the catalyst and reactants, consequently leading to a decrease in CO conversion. The trend of our CO conversion data with increasing space velocity (Fig. 4c) aligns with this behavior. In contrast, catalysts not operating within the reaction-controlled regime (e.g., those governed by external diffusion control) would exhibit increased CO conversion with rising space velocity. Clearly, this contradicts our experimental observations, confirming that our catalyst does not fall under the "not within the reaction-controlled regime" scenario as suggested by the reviewer.

In this way it is worth noting the recent claim (Bettahar, Catal. Rev., 2022; Catalysts, 2024) that the structure of hydrogen spillover in the case of non-reducible oxide supports consists in surface Hδ-/OHδ+ (0<δ<1) pairs resulting from the adsorption of the H spillover species on conjugated Mm+ Op- (p=1 or 2) pairs. The conjugated pairs pre-exist in basic (e.g. MgO) or amphoteric (e.g. alumina) oxide supports. For hydroxylated/acidic supports (silica, alumina, zeolites) they are formed by a dehydroxylation process during the catalyst reduction. The reaction between the hydridic fragment of Hδ-/OHδ+ pairs and CO would produce formate species which are further decomposed to CO and H O by the protonic fragment:
+CO
Mm+Op- + 2 Hspilt <=> M(m- δ)+Hδ- O(p- δ)-Hδ+ => M(m- δ)+HCOO δ- O(p- δ)Hδ+ =>=> Mm+Op- + CO+H O

Author reply: We would like to thank the reviewer for the attention to and interest in the distinctions between our work and conventional confined catalysts. We have added three new examples of metal in confined zeolite to replace the previous examples in the introduction section and have discussed them. Additionally, the description of our innovations compared the previous was constructed a high-RWGS-performance catalyst of Cu@mMOR with the simultaneous inhibition of Ostwald-ripening alongside the migration and aggregation via molecular fence. This had been included in the introduction section (final paragraph) of origin manuscript: “Herein, we proposed to construct Cu@mMOR that encapsulate Cu clusters within mMOR crystals to realize catalytic site separation for CO and H activation in RWGS reaction. For our designed catalyst, mMOR was triggered to crystallize around Cu clusters and encapsulate Cu species insides via its Na+-induced crystallized small pore channels (< 3.0 Å) linking with Cu-O bonds. CO was efficiently captured and activated on outside mMOR, which served as the molecular fence to isolated CO from Cu clusters depended on its small channels. On the other hand, H was dissociated into H* on internal Cu clusters and spillover toward activated CO via Cu-O interface of Cu@mMOR, and finally produced CO with high selectivity. The catalytic site separation strategy significantly enhanced catalytic activation for both CO and H , and rationally changed the CO reaction pathway, thereby effectively preventing Cu Oswald ripening and thermal aggregation in catalysts.”. Revised manuscript, page 3: “For this reaction, Cu-based catalysts are promising non-noble metal candidates for RWGS because of their high hydrogenation activity and high CO selectivity. In general, high temperature during the RWGS reaction usually tends to lead to the sintering of Cu, which can result in catalyst deactivation via the aggregation of Cu NPs. Encapsulating the active metal inside thermally robust zeolites is an effective way to curb high-temperature aggregation. For instance, Xiao et al. embedded Pt NPs within Beta zeolite via a seed-mediated growth route, constructing a rigid “protective shell” around the Pt that markedly suppressed thermal migration and aggregationR31. Likewise, Liu et al. confined sub-nanometer Pt clusters in the straight channels of MEL zeolite, firmly anchoring the naked Pt species and achieving excellent stability in methyl-cyclohexane dehydrogenationR32. These reports confirm that zeolite-confinement can efficiently mitigate thermally induced particle aggregation. However, high-temperature sintering can also proceed via an Ostwald-ripening path, where volatile metal species migrate from interior pores to the outer surface and aggregate. For example, Julian et al. reported that confined Mo zeolite still diffuses outward during high-temperature methane dehydrogenation, causing agglomeration and cokingR33. Analogous to the above catalysts, Cu species are susceptible to forming volatile Cu-carbonyl complexes under CO-rich conditions, leading to significant catalyst deactivationR34. Therefore, the simultaneous inhibition of Ostwald-ripening alongside the migration and aggregation of Cu species in the RWGS reaction remains a crucial challenge for achieving high-performance catalysts that exhibit both efficient activation and enduring stability.”

Author reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding the energy demand of high-temperature RWGS.
First, the ultimate purpose of RWGS is to supply synthesis gas to the mature, downstream Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process. Today’s large-scale syngas is produced predominantly by natural-gas steam reforming or coal gasification, both of which operate under very harsh conditions (≥850 °C and ≥3 MPa) R35, R36. In comparison, RWGS proceeds under much milder temperatures and pressures.
Second, RWGS is an endothermic reaction, and raising the temperature substantially boosts CO conversion. According to the techno-economic analysis, operating at around 600 °C provides the best compromise between conversion and energy inputR37.
Finally, FT synthesis requires a specific H : CO ratio of 0.5 ~ 2R38, R39. Syngas generated at lower RWGS temperatures contains a relatively low CO fraction, which would force the addition of separation or recycle units to adjust the ratio, and these auxiliary units themselves consume significant additional energy.
Revised manuscript, page 3: “The reverse water-gas shift reaction (RWGS) is a desirable and promising CCU technology that catalytically converts CO into syngas under a H environment. Operating the RWGS at atmospheric pressure and temperatures above 500 °C enables direct conversion of CO into syngas with the ideal H /CO ratio for Fischer-Tropsch synthesis, requiring only moderate energy input and avoiding extra downstream separationR37.”

Author reply: We thank the reviewer for the comment regarding whether high temperatures are required for RWGS. The reasons that our system operates at high temperature despite its low apparent activation energy are as follows:
1. Despite RWGS possesses low activation barriers, operation above 450 °C is better to forestall methanation and other side reactions that reduce CO selectivityR40.
2. For Cu@mMOR, the coupled proton-electron transfer that forms the H+/H- pair is the rate-determining step. Elevated temperatures can enhance entropic effects to accelerate H O+ migration within the zeolite channels and thermally activate electron transfer to adjacent orbitalsR41-R43.
3. At high temperatures, Cu@mMOR extensively dissociates H to produce high-energy H+ and electrons whose light mass enables quantum tunneling deep into the zeolite frameworkR44-R46, directly surmounting energy barriers and thus significantly accelerating CO reduction.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I appreciate the authors’ efforts to address the comments raised in my initial review. While some additional data and explanations have been provided, I remain unconvinced by several of the key responses due to insufficiently compelling evidence. Below I elaborate on my continuing concerns regarding the manuscript.
Regarding the reply of Comment 1:
The authors claim to have quantified Cu⁰ and Cu⁺ species based on the white-line peak intensities and their derivatives. However, it is unclear how such quantification was rigorously performed, particularly regarding the assumptions involved and the potential errors in the deconvolution. The method requires further justification, including a clear discussion of quantification accuracy. Additionally, in Supplementary Fig. 14b, the signals attributed to three- and four-membered rings are very weak, raising doubts about their reliability and whether they can robustly support the proposed “molecular fence” effect.
Regarding the reply of Comment 2:
The H₂-TPR peak fitting appears somewhat arbitrary. The authors do not clearly describe the principles used for peak assignment and separation. In particular, how were the peak position and shape corresponding to H-spillover determined? Without a more systematic analysis, the reliability of the deconvolution and the conclusions drawn from it remain questionable.
Regarding the reply of Comment 3:
I am afraid the authors’ explanation for the volcano-type dependence of CO₂ hydrogenation rate on Na⁺ content (Supplementary Fig. 16c) is unconvincing. Regardless of the proposed balance between CO₂ adsorption and surface acidity, the observed trend clearly suggests that Na⁺ is not the primary active site for CO₂ hydrogenation. If Na⁺ were indeed the catalytic site, one would expect a monotonic, positive correlation between Na⁺ content and reaction rate.
Regarding the reply of Comment 4:
The authors interpret the increasing KIE values with temperature as evidence that H⁺/H⁻ migration is the rate-determining step (RDS). This conclusion is ambiguous, as typical H/D KIE values tend to decrease with temperature. Moreover, if the migration of H⁺/H⁻ is indeed the RDS, one would expect the reaction rate to be largely independent of CO₂ partial pressure—yet no evidence is provided to support or refute this. Additionally, the argument that the hydrogenation rates on Cu and Na⁺ cannot be compared is not persuasive. While the Cu and Na⁺ sites are physically separated, kinetic and energetic comparisons remain scientifically valid. Since Cu is a well-known hydrogenation catalyst, the burden of proof lies with the authors to demonstrate that the encapsulated Cu sites are indeed inactive for CO₂ hydrogenation.
Regarding the reply of Comment 5:
The DFT results indicate that direct dissociation of HCOO* has a lower energy barrier than COOH*. However, the authors do not provide clear physical reasoning for this difference. Given the mechanistic importance, I strongly suggest including transition state structures and performing detailed analysis to explain why HCOO* dissociates more readily. This would improve the robustness of the mechanistic proposal.
Regarding the reply of Comment 6:
Zeolites are generally considered insulating materials. The mechanism by which electrons are proposed to migrate through the mordenite framework during hydrogen spillover remains unclear. Although EPR and XPS data were added, a more rigorous discussion on the feasibility of electron conduction in such systems is required. Without further clarification, the fundamental validity of the proposed H⁺/H⁻ transport mechanism remains questionable.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors improved the manuscript for a better understanding of the results obtained. I agree that hydrogen spillover exists and diffuses over the support as H-/H+ pairs. I also agree with the overall reaction paths proposed. For that it merits to be published in Nat. Comm. Nevertheless, at the level of the discussion, the mechanism of diffusion of hydrogen spillover suggested is questionable.
1. According to the authors the initial H-/H+ pairs formed on Cu first become two pairs of H+/e_ entities after the crossing of the interface, then diffuse independently as such on the support and finally recover their H-/H+ identity on the active sites. It is stated that H- is re-formed by recombination of H+ and 2 e-. This is hard to admit.
Is it not more reasonable and simpler to consider that the acid-base nature of the H-/H+ pairs allows easy interactions with and migration on acid-base centers of the support? This was suggested in our previous report.
Hydrogen spillover for non reducible oxides would consist in hydrogenating H/OH pairs (more or less polarized)in vicinal position, formed by an interface dehydroxylation process of OH/OH pairs with water production (Bettahar, Catal. Rev., 2022). After desorption (or reaction) these hydrogenating sites become Mm+/Op-(p=1or2) hydrogen receiving sites. Hydrogenating and receiving sites are denoted as conjugated sites. It comes that the diffusion of hydrogen spillover necessarily proceeds by migration of H/H pairs from Mm+ O- site to Mm+ O- site (Bettahar, Catalysts, 2024).
In the presence of Na+ the hydrogenating sites are deprotonated and this favors the adsorption of CO2 (see suggested reaction paths in attached file)
This mechanism is compatible with the physical characterization of the catalysts, notably with the DRIFTS experiments (Figure 34). Indeed, after adsorbing CO2 the introduction of H2 led to concomitant formation of acidic OH groups, Al-H hydrides and adsorbed water which may correspond to the formation of the AlH/SiOH hydrogenating sites (water may arose from both dehydroxylation and WGSR processes).
2. In these DRIFTS experiments the authors evidenced the existence of hydrogen spillover during the hydrogenation reaction. Why? Do they assume that hydrogen spillover is induced by the presence of the organic molecule (see Choi et al., Nanoresearch, 2022)? If it is such the statement is wrong because H spiltover species are incorporated in the support in the absence of any organic molecule, as the authors know. Why DRIFTS experiments were not conducted in H2 atmosphere solely?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: The responses address the reviewer's comments and the revised manuscript is recommended for acceptance.

[II] We thank the reviewers for their insightful comments. To further support the proposed “molecular fence” hypothesis, we conducted additional positron annihilation spectroscopy (PAS) and N O chemisorption/temperature-programmed reduction (TPR) 2 experiments, which provide more direct evidence to elucidate the mechanism. The PAS characterization confirms the presence of ultra-micropores closely surrounding the Cu nanoclusters. 4. The authors interpret the increasing KIE values with temperature as evidence that H+/H- migration is the rate-determining step (RDS). This conclusion is ambiguous, as typical H/D KIE values tend to decrease with temperature. Moreover, if the migration of H+/H- is indeed the RDS, one would expect the reaction rate to be largely independent of CO partial pressure—yet no evidence is provided to support or refute this. 2 Additionally, the argument that the hydrogenation rates on Cu and Na+ cannot be compared is not persuasive. While the Cu and Na+ sites are physically separated, kinetic and energetic comparisons remain scientifically valid. Since Cu is a well-known hydrogenation catalyst, the burden of proof lies with the authors to demonstrate that the encapsulated Cu sites are indeed inactive for CO hydrogenation. 2
Author reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s constructive questions. We have addressed these concerns in the following three points.
[I]. First, regarding the reviewer’s comment that “the increasing KIE values with temperature as evidence that H+/H- migration is the rate-determining step (RDS). This conclusion is ambiguous, as typical H/D KIE values tend to decrease with temperature”, we fully agree with this assessment. According to relevant reviews, the kinetic isotope effect (KIE) is generally considered to be governed by both the difference in zero-point energy (ZPE) and the tunneling effectR19. Generally, as the temperature increases, atomic motion intensifies, and the contribution of the ZPE difference to the KIE gradually diminishes, resulting in a decrease in the apparent KIE valuesR20. However, the quantum tunneling effect can be significantly enhanced in specific environments, such as structures rich in weak-interaction donors/acceptors or hydrogen-bond networks where hydrogen atoms resideR21-R24. This enhancement can consequently lead to an increase in KIER25, R26.
In the Cu@mMOR system, we observed that CO conversion increased with 2 temperature. This process also generated more dissociated hydrogen species and water molecules. Since these water molecules are confined within the zeolite channels, we believe they interact weakly with spillover hydrogen species. This interaction creates favorable conditions for hydrogen tunneling. Accordingly, we have clarified the KIE mechanism in the revised manuscript and highlighted the relevant sections.

[III]. We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to supplement the kinetic and energetic analyses of CO hydrogenation over encapsulated Cu clusters. To theoretically address 2 the concerns regarding the activity of Cu sites, a Cu@mMOR model based on the cleaved MOR surface was constructed (i.e., the Cu clusters situated on the MOR cleavage plane) and performed detailed DFT calculations in the attachment. This model was employed to compare the kinetic and energetic differences between the encapsulated Cu clusters and the active sites of mMOR. Our calculations indicate that although the Cu clusters in Cu@mMOR can theoretically catalyze CO hydrogenation 2 via the carboxyl pathway, their strong interaction with C atoms favors the formation of copper carbonyl species, which subsequently induces Ostwald ripening and accelerates catalyst deactivation. This reveals a strong interaction between the Cu clusters and the C atoms of carbon-containing species (e.g., COOH and CO) during the reaction. According to the transition-state/adsorption-strength scaling relationsR35, R36, this strong Cu-C interaction effectively lowers the transition state barrier, thereby establishing the thermodynamic and kinetic dominance of the carboxyl pathway.
However, this excessively strong CO adsorption also implies that Cu species are 2 highly susceptible to Ostwald ripening under high-temperature reaction conditions, which serves as a critical consideration in our catalyst design. Most critically, DRIFTS spectroscopy (Fig. 5d in the manuscript) has confirmed that Cu@mMOR follows the formate pathway, which stands in stark contrast to the DFT-derived conclusion that the carboxyl pathway is preferred on Cu clusters. This fundamental mechanistic contradiction provides compelling evidence that the active sites for CO hydrogenation 2 in Cu@mMOR are not the encapsulated Cu clusters, but rather the mMOR framework sites.”

5. The DFT results indicate that direct dissociation of HCOO* has a lower energy barrier than COOH*. However, the authors do not provide clear physical reasoning for this difference. Author reply: We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion. We have supplemented detailed transition state structures in the revised supplementary information.
Furthermore, we added crystal orbital Hamilton population (COHP) and independent gradient model based on Hirshfeld partition (IGMH) analyses to reveal the physical origin of this differenceR37-R41. Our analysis indicated that the higher dissociation energy barrier for COOH* primarily stemmed from three factors: (1) the necessity of breaking an additional Al-H bond to facilitate electron transfer; (2) the significant antibonding character of the transition state C≡O bond near the Fermi level, as revealed by COHP; and (3) the strong hydrogen bonding interactions between the initial state hydroxyl group and the framework oxygen, as confirmed by IGMH, which increased the difficulty of dissociation. These revisions were integrated into the main text. Additionally, detailed explanations, figures, and animations were included in the revised supplementary information. All changes were highlighted in yellow, as shown below:

Protonation is kinetically much more favorable, with a very low barrier of only 0.43 eV, leading easily to HCOOH formation. In contrast, direct dissociation pathways face much higher barriers (1.72 eV for HCOO⁻ and 2.04 eV for COOH⁺), making them far less likely. These substantial barriers (particularly for COOH+) were attributed to the necessity of rupturing an additional Al-H bond to facilitate electron transfer, strong antibonding orbital repulsion, and the requirement to overcome hydrogen bonding interactions (Supplementary Fig. 53-54 and Supplementary Movies 11-14) R37-R41. 6. Zeolites are generally considered insulating materials. The mechanism by which electrons are proposed to migrate through the mordenite framework during hydrogen spillover remains unclear. Author reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We acknowledge that the poor electrical conductivity of zeolites was not fully accounted for in our original manuscript. Consequently, the previous hypothesis proposing the “separate transport of protons and electrons over the zeolite framework” was physically unsound, and we have now rectified this interpretation. To rigorously elucidate the hydrogen spillover mechanism within the Cu@mMOR system, we have replaced the original H -DRIFTS data with steady-state isotopic transient kinetic analysis (SSITKA) 2 using H /D switching. By coupling SSITKA with in situ FTIR spectroscopy, we have 2 2 confirmed that hydrogen spillover in Cu@mMOR is primarily mediated by the dynamic coordination of H+/H- pairs within the zeolite channels. Accordingly, the manuscript and supplementary information have been updated with revised text and new experimental data. We have also corrected the interpretations of the previous in situ EPR and XPS results to align with this mechanism. All modifications are highlighted in yellow, as detailed below:
Revised manuscript, page 20-21:“To unravel the chemical nature and dynamic behavior of hydrogen spillover at the molecular level, the evolution of hydrogen-containing species on Cu@mMOR were monitored using steady-state isotopic transient kinetic analysis coupled with FTIR (SSITKA-FTIR) during H /D switching. The coexistence of these H+ and H- species provided direct evidence for the heterolytic cleavage of H on 2 Cu@mMOR and identifies the specific nature of the resulting fragments. Upon switching the feed to D , the intensities of these hydrogenated species gradually 2 decayed, with a concomitant growth of deuterated species peaks at the lower wavenumbersR44, R45. This rapid H/D isotopic exchange demonstrated that the generated H+/H- pairs exhibited high mobility and dynamic exchange activity over the framework acid-base sitesR49, R50.
Next, in situ EPR was carried out to investigate the electronic mechanism driving H 2 heterolytic activation. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 37, Cu@mMOR displayed a strong signal associated with unpaired electrons on the Cu clusters under H feeding R46. 2 When the atmosphere was switched to CO /H , this EPR signal decreased markedly. 2 2 This indicated that the electrons were transferred to adsorbed hydrogen to generate H- species, which subsequently migrate into the channels and participate in the RWGS reaction. Furthermore, XPS analysis was conducted to elucidate the migration and consumption dynamics of hydrogen species by monitoring valence shifts of Cu and Al in Cu@mMOR under H and CO /H atmospheres. As depicted in Supplementary Fig. 2 2 2 38, H treatment decreased the binding energies of both Cu and Al to indicate an 2 electron-rich state, whereas the subsequent introduction of CO /H triggered a 2 2 synchronous positive shift in these valuesR47, R48. ## Abstract

The conversion of CO into high-value syngas (CO and H ) using Cu-based catalysts has garnered
2 2
considerable interest. However, these catalysts deactivate rapidly due to Ostwald-ripening and thermal
aggregation. Herein, we propose to encapsulate Cu-cluster into mMOR zeolite for engineering a
separation-site catalyst Cu@mMOR. In the reverse water-gas shift reaction (RWGS), mMOR zeolite of
Cu@mMOR directly captures and then activates CO , and simultaneously serves as a molecular fence to
2
prevent CO contact with Cu-clusters surrounding with small pore of mMOR (< 3.0 Å) channels. These
2
encapsulated Cu-clusters in mMOR possess considerable Cu vacancies, which significantly facilitate H
2
heterolytic dissociation, transferring H* species towNards activated CO
2
on mMOR and converting them
into CO. This separation-site strategy efficientl y increases catalytic activation while intelligently altering
2
the CO reaction pathway, preventing Cu from thermal agglomeration and Oswald ripening in the catalyst.
2
Consequently, Cu@mMOR attainTs a space-time yield of CO as high as 3290 mmol g -1 h-1, with catalytic
cat
stability extending up to 7A88 hours.

---

## Introduction

The ongoing and excessive emissions of CO have led to global climate change, which is currently
2
receiving considerable attention. The conversion of CO into high-value chemicals is essential for
2
mitigating the greenhouse effect and maintaining a sustainable environment and energy supply1. Among
these, syngas (CO and H mixture) is reported to be an essential chemical used in the large-scale
2
production of alcohols, esters, and liquid fuels2. Recently, the insufficient provision stemming from
reliance solely on fossil resources has spurred growing interest in catalytic CO hydrogenation-a
2
promising strategy for converting greenhouse gases into valuable syngas3. Despite its apparent appeal,
this approach presents formidable obstacles.

The reverse water-gas shift reaction (RWG S) is a desirable and promising CCU technology that
catalytically converts CO into syngas under a H environment. Operating the RWGS at atmospheric
2 C 2
pressure and temperatures abovTe 500 °C enables direct conversion of CO into syngas with the ideal
2
H /CO ratio for Fischer-TAropsch synthesis, requiring only moderate energy input and avoiding extra
2
downstream separation4. For this reaction, Cu-based catalysts are promising non-noble metal candidates
for RWGS because of their high hydrogenation activity and high CO selectivity5. In general, high
temperature during the RWGS reaction usually tends to lead to the sintering of Cu, which can result in
catalyst deactivation via the aggregation of Cu NPs. Encapsulating the active metal inside thermally robust
zeolites is an effective way to curb high-temperature aggregation. For instance, Xiao et al. embedded Pt
NPs within Beta zeolite via a seed-mediated growth route, constructing a rigid “protective shell” around
the Pt that markedly suppressed thermal migration and aggregation6. Likewise, Liu et al. confined sub-
nanometer Pt clusters in the straight channels of MEL zeolite, firmly anchoring the naked Pt species and
achieving excellent stability in methyl-cyclohexane dehydrogenation7. These reports confirm that zeolite-
confinement can efficiently mitigate thermally induced particle aggregation. However, high-temperature
sintering can also proceed via an Ostwald-ripening path, where volatile metal species migrate from
interior pores to the outer surface and aggregate. For example, Julian et al. reported that confined Mo
zeolite still diffuses outward during high-temperature methane dehydrogenation, causing agglomeration
and coking8. Analogous to the above catalysts, Cu species are susceptible to forming volatile Cu-carbonyl
complexes under CO-rich conditions, leading to significant catalyst deactivation9. Therefore, the
simultaneous inhibition of Ostwald-ripening alongside the migration and aggregation of Cu species in the
RWGS reaction remains a crucial challenge for acNhieving high-performance catalysts that exhibit both
efficient activation and enduring stability.

Herein, we proposed to construct Cu@mMOR (copper-encapsulated modified mordenite zeolite) that
encapsulate Cu clusters within TmMOR (modified mordenite zeolite) crystals to realize catalytic site
separation for CO and H A activation in RWGS reaction. For our designed catalyst, mMOR was triggered
2 2
to crystallize around Cu clusters and encapsulate Cu species insides via its Na+-induced crystallized small
pore channels (< 3.0 Å) linking with Cu-O bonds. CO was efficiently captured and activated on outside
2
mMOR, which served as the molecular fence to isolated CO from Cu clusters depended on its small
2
channels. On the other hand, H was dissociated into H* on internal Cu clusters and spillover toward
2
activated CO via Cu-O interface of Cu@mMOR, and finally produced CO with high selectivity. The
2
catalytic site separation strategy significantly enhanced catalytic activation for both CO and H , and
2 2
rationally changed the CO reaction pathway, thereby effectively preventing Cu Oswald ripening and
2
thermal aggregation in catalysts. Therefore, a space-time yield of 3290 mmol g -1 h-1 was attained in
cat
Cu@mMOR at high-temperature conditions (600 °C), showcasing the long-term stability of catalyst
performance over a duration of 788 hours (49.1% CO -conversion-rate and 99.6% CO-selectivity).
2

## Results

Design idea and synthesis strategy for Cu@mMOR
Fig. 1 showed our design idea and the corresponding synthesis strategy for mMOR-confined Cu catalyst
(denoted as Cu@mMOR) having separated catalytic sites for H and CO . Firstly, SiO nanospheres were
2 2 2
used to encapsulate Cu-based precursor via a reversed-phase micro-emulsion method (seen Fig. 1a-b).
Next, Cu-based precursor were calcined and reduced into Cu particles surrounding with SiO (named
2
Cu@SiO ,Fig. 1c). In this process, Na+ was used as a directing agent to induce the growth of small Si-O
2
cages (< 3.0 Å) in mMOR to isolate CO from Cu species. Next, the whole part of SiO of Cu@SiO was
2 2 2
gradually converted into mMOR zeolite under the iNnduction of N-methyl-pyrrolidine and followed by the
second calcination and H reduction (seen Fig. 1d-f and Supplementary Fig. 1). Finally, a portion of Na+
2
was selectively retained while the remainder was converted to NH + via low-concentration NH Cl
4 4
exchange, followed by calcinatioTn to ultimately form H⁺, resulting in the formation of Cu@mMOR.

Morphology of different Cu-based catalysts
It is evident from Fig. 2a-b that Cu@mMOR contained numerous Cu black dots (1.5 ± 0.3 nm) that were
homogenously dispersed throughout the nanosheets. These amorphous Cu nanodots were encapsulated in
mMOR, which was identified by the lattice fringes of (110) plane10 (Fig. 2c). According to the elemental
energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)-mapping images depicted in Fig. 2d, the Cu element was
homogeneously distributed throughout the mMOR zeolite. However, the particle size of Cu in spherical
Cu@SiO (~20 nm, Fig. 2e) was about ~2.1 nm (Fig. 2f), which was obviously larger than that in
2
Cu@mMOR. It can be inferred that Cu was further reduced into smaller clusters in a confined space
during the crystal transformation from SiO to mMOR. In contrast, Cu-impregnated mMOR (denoted as
2
Cu/mMOR) contained nano-sized particles of approximately 4.4 nm on its outer surface of mMOR (Fig.
2g), and these nanoparticles displayed distinct lattice patterns corresponding to the metallic Cu (111)
crystal plane11 (Fig. 2h). It can be seen that the copper acetylacetonate impregnation method proved
challenging for incorporating Cu nanoparticles into mMOR crystals and effectively controlling their
particle size within mMOR.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) and X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyses (Supplementary Fig. 2 and
Supplementary Table 1) revealed that Cu/mMOR and Cu@mMOR had high crystallinity of MOR type
zeolite, whereas Cu@SiO showed a diffuse X-ray peak of amorphous silica phase. This indicated that
2
the amorphous silica nanosphere was completely transformed into a highly crystalline MOR zeolite
structure in Cu@mMOR12. In addition, non e of the three catalysts (Cu@SiO , Cu/mMOR, and
2
Cu@mMOR) showed clear diffraction peaks of Cu crystals. However, the Cu element detected in XRF
(Supplementary Table 1) had aT very similar percentage composition in the range of 2.6-4.1 wt.%,
suggesting that Cu speciAes were highly dispersed in these catalysts. Additionally, the XPS survey
(Supplementary Fig. 3) showed the slight presence of Na element in Cu@mMOR but not in Cu/mMOR,
implying that the former remains some Na+ sites. Moreover, the Cu 2p XPS patterns of Cu@mMOR and
Cu@SiO exhibited much lower peak area than that of impregnated Cu/mMOR (Supplementary Fig. 4),
2
suggesting the extensive encapsulation of Cu nanoparticles rather than their exposure on the MOR
external surface13. Next, the pore texture (Supplementary Fig. 5 and Supplementary Table 2) of
Cu@mMOR showed a slight reduction in N adsorption uptake (427.1 m2 g-1) of type I isotherm compared
2
to that of pure mMOR (530.1 m2 g-1). This meant that most of the micropore structure of mMOR
maintained upon encapsulating Cu nanoparticles in mMOR. In contrast, Cu/mMOR exhibited a lower
surface area of 310.7 m2 g-1, indicating a partial loss of the mMOR porous structure due to the obstruction
caused by the impregnated Cu nanoparticles14. As anticipated, Cu@SiO had minimal porous structures
2
attributed to the low porosity of SiO . The textural structure analysis inferred that Cu@mMOR maintained
2
the mMOR porous property after encapsulating Cu species with homogeneous distribution, which would
favor the adsorption and transport of reactants and active species during the reaction. Further, positron
annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS) was conducted to determine the pore size distribution of the
ultra-microporous region in MOR, mMOR, and their Cu-based catalysts15. The deconvoluted PALS
spectra display four distinct peaks corresponding to different positron annihilation lifetimes (τ -τ ;
1 4
Supplementary Fig. 6a). An increase in τ value indNicates larger pore sizes within the MOR framework.
Here, τ denotes the bulk lifetime, which is attrib uted to direct annihilation within the non-porous regions16.
1
The remaining lifetimes τ -τ correspond to positron annihilation within the 5-membered, 8-membered,
2 4
and 12-membered ring channels Tof MOR, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 6b-c). In comparison to the
support, the τ componenAts associated with 8-MRs exhibited distinctly opposite trends in Cu@mMOR
3
and Cu/mMOR. Specifically, the calculated pore size for Cu/mMOR increased to 3.6 Å. This observation
aligns with the pore-blocking effect identified via N adsorption isotherms (Supplementary Fig. 5),
2
ascribed to the obstruction of pore mouths by external Cu particles. Thus, it compels positrons to
annihilate within larger inter-particle voids on the surface17. In contrast, the encapsulation strategy yielded
a shrunken pore size of 2.8 Å for Cu@mMOR, directly confirming the effective occupation of the 8-MR
channels by Cu species. Furthermore, coincidence doppler broadening (CDB) analysis revealed a higher
electron density for Cu@mMOR in the low-momentum valence electron region (< 4×10-3 m c;
0
Supplementary Fig. 7), corroborating the tight confinement of copper clusters within the unique micro-
environment constructed by the 5-MRs and 8-MRs18. Notably, this shrunken pore mouths of Cu@mMOR
(2.8 Å) precisely matches the kinetic diameter of H (2.8 Å) while remains smaller than that of CO (3.3
2 2
Å)19. Conceptually, this double-ring encapsulation architecture could act as a "molecular fence" for
suppressing thermal aggregation and Ostwald ripening via the spatial separation of CO and H .

Structural characterization of different Cu-based catalysts
To better understand the local structure of Cu species in different micro-environments, X-ray absorption
spectroscopy (XAS) was performed in order to evaluate the Cu chemical state and coordination status in
various catalysts. The edge energy of the two catalysts (Cu@mMOR and Cu/mMOR) at the Cu K-edge
(Fig. 3a) was positioned between the Cu foil and CuN2 O standards, with no pre-edge band of Cu2+ detected

two catalysts20. Compared to Cu/mMOR, Cu@mMOR exhibited a much higher Cu adsorption edge
energy, attributing to a higher proTportion of Cu+ species in Cu@mMOR21. To quantify the Cu+ species in
the catalyst, a mathematicAal relationship between the absorption edge energy position and the valence
state was established by fitting data from the corresponding standards22, 23. As shown in Supplementary
Fig. 8, the Cu+ content in Cu@mMOR was calculated to be ⁓38.1 at.%. In contrast, the Cu+ proportions

2
higher Cu+ content in Cu@mMOR is indicative of enhanced interfacial charge transfer from Cu0 to
mMOR, a process facilitated by the abundant interfaces inherent to the encapsulation structure.

The local coordination environment of Cu species in various catalysts was identified by fitting the
Fourier transform extended X-ray absorption fine structure (FT-EXAFS) of the various catalysts, as

Moreover, the types and contents of defects in Cu clusters within Cu@mMOR were investigated via

In comparison, Cu/mMOR displayed a negligible peak of defective Cu-O around Cu vacancies at 218 cm-

had a much higher concentration of Cu vacancies than Cu/mMOR, which was attributed to the Cu-O

(Supplementary Fig. 10) were also measured for Cu@mMOR and Cu@SiO . As observed, the defective

It has been reported that Cu vacancies can significantly influence the redox properties of catalysts30, 31.
Furthermore, H temperature-pTrogrammed reduction-mass spectrometry (H -TPR-MS) analyses of

Cu@mMOR and Cu/mMOR. As shown, hydrogen reduction profile of Cu@mMOR exhibited a single

2

Cu@mMOR37.

The effects of Cu diverse microenvironment within prepared Cu-based catalysts on their catalytic activity
